title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: By now, no one remained in the reception room except Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, who sat beneath the portrait of Catherine the Great, talking urgently. The moment they saw Pierre and his companion, they fell silent. Pierre thought he caught the princess hiding something as she whispered:
"I can't stand the sight of that woman."
"Catiche has had tea set up in the small drawing room," Prince Vasili told Anna Mikhaylovna. "Go and have something, my poor Anna Mikhaylovna, or you won't hold up."
To Pierre he said nothing, only gave his arm a sympathetic squeeze below the shoulder. Pierre followed Anna Mikhaylovna into the small drawing room.

"There is nothing quite so refreshing after a sleepless night as a cup of this delicious Russian tea," Lorrain was saying with restrained animation, standing and sipping from a delicate Chinese handleless cup before a table set with tea things and a cold supper in the small circular room. Everyone who was at Count Bezukhov's house that night had gathered here to fortify themselves. Pierre remembered this circular drawing room with its mirrors and small tables well. During balls at the house, Pierre—who didn't know how to dance—used to like sitting here, watching the ladies pass through in their ball gowns with diamonds and pearls on bare shoulders, admiring themselves in the brilliantly lit mirrors that multiplied their reflections. Now the same room was dimly lit by only two candles. On a small table, the tea things and supper dishes stood in disarray, and in the middle of the night a mixed group of people sat there—not celebrating but whispering somberly, every word and gesture showing that none of them could forget what was happening, and was about to happen, in the bedroom. Pierre ate nothing, though he very much wanted to. He looked inquiringly at his guide and saw that she was once again tiptoeing toward the reception room where they had left Prince Vasili and the eldest princess. Pierre decided this too must be essential, and after a short pause, followed her. Anna Mikhaylovna was standing beside the princess, and the two women were speaking in agitated whispers.
"Let me be the judge, Princess, of what is necessary and what is not," said the younger of the two, clearly in the same state of agitation as when she had slammed her door.

"But my dear princess," Anna Mikhaylovna answered calmly but firmly, positioning herself to block the way to the bedroom and prevent the other woman from passing, "won't this be too much for poor Uncle at a moment when he needs rest? Worldly matters at a time when his soul is already prepared..."

Prince Vasili sat in an armchair in his usual pose, one leg crossed high over the other. His flabby cheeks—which looked heavier at the bottom—were twitching violently, but he wore the air of a man unconcerned with what the two ladies were saying.
"Come now, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna, let Catiche do as she wishes. You know how fond the count is of her."

"I don't even know what's in this document," said the younger woman, turning to Prince Vasili and pointing at the inlaid portfolio in her hand. "All I know is that his real will is in his writing desk, and this is just a paper he's forgotten about...."
She tried to get past Anna Mikhaylovna, but Anna Mikhaylovna sprang forward to block her path.

"I know, my dear, kind princess," Anna Mikhaylovna said, gripping the portfolio so tightly it was obvious she would not let go easily. "Dear princess, I beg you, I implore you—have some pity on him! [Speaking in French] I beseech you..."

The princess said nothing. The only sounds were their struggle over the portfolio. But it was clear that if the princess did speak, her words would not be kind to Anna Mikhaylovna. Despite her tenacious grip, Anna Mikhaylovna's voice lost none of its honeyed firmness and softness.
"Pierre, my dear, come here. I think he won't be out of place in a family discussion—don't you agree, Prince?"

"Why don't you speak, cousin?" the princess suddenly shrieked, so loudly that the people in the drawing room heard and were startled. "Why are you standing there in silence while heaven knows who takes it upon herself to interfere—making a scene on the very threshold of a dying man's room? You schemer!" she hissed viciously, and yanked the portfolio with all her might.
But Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward to maintain her grip and adjusted her hold.
Prince Vasili rose from his chair. "Oh!" he said with reproach and surprise. "This is absurd! Come, let go, I tell you."
The princess released her grip.
"And you too!"
But Anna Mikhaylovna did not obey.
"Let go, I tell you! I'll take responsibility. I'll go in and ask him myself. I!... Is that good enough for you?"

"But, Prince," said Anna Mikhaylovna, "after such a solemn sacrament, give him a moment's peace! Here, Pierre, tell them what you think," she said, turning to the young man, who had come close and was staring in astonishment at the princess's furious face—stripped of all dignity—and at Prince Vasili's twitching cheeks.
"Remember, you will answer for the consequences," Prince Vasili said severely. "You don't know what you're doing."
"Vile woman!" the princess shouted, lunging unexpectedly at Anna Mikhaylovna and snatching the portfolio from her hands.
Prince Vasili bowed his head and spread his hands in a helpless gesture.

At that moment, the terrible door—which Pierre had watched for so long, and which had always opened so quietly—burst open with a bang against the wall, and the second of the three sisters rushed out, wringing her hands.
"What are you doing!" she cried desperately. "He's dying, and you leave me alone with him!"

The eldest sister dropped the portfolio. Anna Mikhaylovna swooped down, snatched up the contested object, and ran into the bedroom. The eldest princess and Prince Vasili, recovering their composure, hurried after her. A few minutes later, the eldest sister emerged with a pale, rigid face, biting her lower lip again. When she caught sight of Pierre, her expression showed undisguised hatred.
"Yes, now you can celebrate!" she said. "This is what you've been waiting for." Then she burst into tears, covered her face with her handkerchief, and rushed from the room.

Prince Vasili came out next. He staggered to the sofa where Pierre was sitting and collapsed onto it, covering his face with his hand. Pierre noticed he was pale, and that his jaw was trembling and shaking as though he had a fever.

"Oh, my friend!" he said, gripping Pierre by the elbow. There was a sincerity and vulnerability in his voice that Pierre had never heard before. "How often we sin, how much we deceive—and for what? I'm nearly sixty, my dear friend... I too... It all ends in death. Death is terrible..." And he burst into tears.
Anna Mikhaylovna was the last to come out. She approached Pierre with slow, quiet steps.
"Pierre!" she said.
Pierre looked at her questioningly. She leaned forward and kissed the young man on his forehead, wetting him with her tears. After a pause, she said:
"He is gone...."
Pierre stared at her over his spectacles.
"Come, I'll go with you. Try to cry—nothing brings such relief as tears."

She led him into the dark drawing room, and Pierre was grateful that no one could see his face. Anna Mikhaylovna left him there, and when she returned, he had fallen asleep with his head resting on his arm.
The next morning, Anna Mikhaylovna said to Pierre:

"Yes, my dear, this is a great loss for all of us—to say nothing of you. But God will sustain you. You are young, and now, I hope, the master of an immense fortune. The will hasn't been opened yet. I know you well enough to be certain this won't go to your head, but it does impose responsibilities on you, and you must be a man."
Pierre said nothing.

"Perhaps I'll tell you someday, my dear boy, that if I hadn't been there, God only knows what would have happened. You know, your uncle promised me just the day before yesterday not to forget Boris. But he didn't have time. I hope, my dear friend, that you'll carry out your father's wishes?"

Pierre understood none of this and, blushing with embarrassment, looked at Princess Anna Mikhaylovna in silence. After her conversation with Pierre, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to the Rostovs' and went to bed. When she woke up the next morning, she told the Rostovs and all her acquaintances the details of Count Bezukhov's death. She said the count had died just as she herself would wish to die—that his end was not only moving but spiritually uplifting. As for the final meeting between father and son, it was so touching she could hardly think of it without tears, and she couldn't say who had shown more grace in those terrible moments—the father, who had remembered everyone at the last and spoken such tender words to his son, or Pierre, whose grief was heartbreaking to witness, though he had tried so hard to hide it to spare his dying father. "It's painful, but it does the soul good. It elevates you to see men like the old count and his worthy son," she said. About the eldest princess and Prince Vasili, she spoke disapprovingly—but only in whispers, and as a great secret.
